title: Hello, Termux
summary: Look around a fresh Termux home directory and read your first flag.
objective: Read the file in your home directory to capture the flag.
briefing:
You are dropped into the Termux home directory. Two commands do most of the work here:

- `ls` lists what is in the current directory.
- `cat <file>` prints a file to the screen.

List the directory, find the interesting file, and read it.

Welcome to Learmux!
Your first flag is: TERMUX{hello_world}

title: Hidden in Plain Sight
summary: Unix hides files whose names start with a dot. Find one.
objective: Find and read the hidden file in your home directory.
briefing: On Unix-like systems a leading dot marks a file as hidden — `ls` will not show it by default. Use `ls -a` to list *all* entries, then `cat` the one that looks suspicious.

notes.txt.content: Remember to check for dotfiles next time.

title: Follow the Trail
summary: A flag is buried deep in a directory tree. Hunt it down.
objective: Locate the file named flag.txt anywhere under your home directory and read it.
briefing:
The flag is several directories deep. Instead of `cd`-ing one level at a time, let `find` do the walking:

```
find . -name flag.txt
```

Then `cat` the path it prints.
hints: `cd` and `ls` work too if you prefer.

title: World-Writable
summary: Spot the file that any user on the system can write to.
objective: Find the one file whose permissions are rw-rw-rw- and read it.
briefing:
`ls -l` shows a permissions column like `-rw-r--r--`. Read it as three groups: **user**, **group**, **others**. A file that is `rw-rw-rw-` (octal `666`) can be written by *anyone* — a classic security smell.

List the directory in long form and find the file that is too permissive.
hints: Look for `-rw-rw-rw-` — that is the odd one out.

title: Logs Never Lie
summary: A flag is buried in a noisy access log. Grep it out.
objective: Search access.log for the flag.
briefing: `grep <pattern> <file>` prints only the lines that match. The log is hundreds of lines of noise, but the flag starts with `TERMUX{` — search for that.

title: Case Insensitive
summary: Match a pattern regardless of letter case.
objective: Find the line containing the flag without worrying about case.
briefing: The flag is in `notes.txt`, but the author wrote surrounding text in mixed case. `grep -i` ignores case, so `grep -i termux notes.txt` will find `TERMUX{...}` too.

title: Pipe Dreams
summary: Chain commands together with the pipe operator.
objective: Extract the third field of the admin line in users.txt.
briefing:
The pipe `|` sends the output of one command into the next. A passwd-style file is colon-separated; `cut -d: -f3` prints the third field.

```
cat users.txt | grep admin | cut -d: -f3
```

title: Decode Me
summary: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Decode it.
objective: Decode encoded.txt to reveal the flag.
briefing:
Base64 turns binary into printable text. It is trivially reversible:

```
base64 -d encoded.txt
```
hints: The `-d` flag decodes instead of encodes.

title: ROT13 Is Weak
summary: A Caesar cipher with a shift of 13. Undo it.
objective: Decode cipher.txt to reveal the flag.
briefing:
ROT13 rotates every letter 13 places. It is its own inverse. The Learmux shell ships a helper:

```
rot13 cipher.txt
```
hints: Applying it twice returns the original.

title: Hex on the Wire
summary: Inspect raw bytes with a hex dump.
objective: Hex-dump data.bin and read the flag from the ASCII column.
briefing:
`xxd` prints each byte as hex, with the printable characters shown on the right. Even when a file looks like gibberish, the ASCII column often gives it away:

```
xxd data.bin
```
hints: The right-hand column of `xxd` shows printable characters.
`strings data.bin` pulls the flag out in one piece.

title: Integrity Matters
summary: Two backups look identical. A checksum tells them apart.
objective: Find which file matches the digest in checksum.txt, then read it.
briefing: A SHA-256 digest is a fingerprint for file contents. `checksum.txt` records the digest of the *genuine* file. Compute the digest of both candidates with `sha256sum` and compare.
hints: The file whose digest matches checksum.txt is the real one.

title: Environment Leak
summary: Secrets are often left behind in environment variables.
objective: Inspect the environment and find the leaked secret.
briefing: Environment variables are handed to every process a shell starts. That makes them a common place for secrets to leak. Print them with `env` (or `printenv`).

title: Process Hunt
summary: A careless admin left a secret in a running command line.
objective: List running processes and find the flag in a command argument.
briefing: On real systems, `ps` shows the full command line of every process — including secrets people pass as arguments by mistake. Run `ps` here and read carefully.

ps-notes.txt.content: Never pass secrets as command-line arguments.

title: Package Cache
summary: A suspicious package is installed. List packages and read its metadata.
objective: List the installed packages and find the flag in the metadata.
briefing:
Termux uses `pkg` to manage software. Listing installed packages can reveal unexpected or malicious tools:

```
pkg list-installed
```
hints: The flag is in the description of `termux-flagutils`.

title: User Accounts
summary: Read the account database and find an unusual user.
objective: Read the account database at /etc/accounts and find the flag in a user record.
briefing: `/etc/accounts` lists user accounts as colon-separated records: `name:password:uid:gid:GECOS:home:shell`. Read it with `cat`.
hints: One GECOS field holds the flag.

title: Network Recon
summary: Scan a host and read a service banner that leaks a flag.
objective: Run an nmap scan against 127.0.0.1 and read the service banner.
briefing:
`nmap` maps open ports and, with service detection, reads the banner each service returns. Banners are a classic information leak.

```
nmap -sV 127.0.0.1
```
hints: Look at the banner for port 1337.

title: Fetch the Flag
summary: Pull a flag down from a web endpoint.
objective: Use curl to fetch http://challenge.local/flag and read the response.
briefing:
`curl <url>` prints the body of an HTTP response to the terminal. Fetch the challenge endpoint:

```
curl http://challenge.local/flag
```
hints: Use curl against the challenge endpoint.
wget can also download the file.

title: Buried Strings
summary: Extract readable text from a messy binary blob.
objective: Use strings on firmware.bin to reveal the embedded flag.
briefing:
`strings` pulls out runs of printable characters from any file. It is the first thing a forensics analyst runs on an unknown blob:

```
strings firmware.bin
```
hints: The flag is one of several printable runs.

title: Reverse Engineering
summary: A file holds the flag written backwards.
objective: Reverse the characters in reversed.txt to read the flag.
briefing:
Not every obfuscation is cryptography. `rev` reverses each line — perfect for text stored backwards:

```
rev reversed.txt
```
hints: `cat` then read it right-to-left also works.

title: The Final Boss
summary: Combine grep, cut and base64 in one pipeline to win.
objective: Extract the base64 blob from capture.log and decode it.
briefing:
A service logged its flag base64-encoded, buried in a busy log. Chain the tools you have learned:

```
grep flag_blob capture.log | cut -d" " -f4 | base64 -d
```

Breaking it down: `grep` finds the line, `cut` takes the fourth field, `base64 -d` decodes it.
hints: The blob is the fourth whitespace-separated field.
